The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor

Maosen Zhang, Jianshuo Dong, Yutong Zhang, Affiliation: Tsinghua University Email: qiuhan@tsinghua.edu.cn    Jie Zhang, Tianwei Zhang, and Han Qiu Affiliation:  Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Affiliation: SiliconProspect AI Email: zms25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the show-up attack, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems to scale up the test-time compute and solve more complex tasks (Qian et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). Among many designs, the centralized multi-agent architecture is popular and representative, where a supervisor agent is responsible for ruling a swarm of subagents (Dang et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2025; Zhu et al., 2026). While many works have empirically demonstrated the benefits of such centralized architecture (Fourney et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Adimulam et al., 2026), such a design inevitably leads to a new vulnerability. The supervisor agent relies on its underlying subagents to be faithful and convey trustworthy subtask results, but what if subagents intentionally deceive their supervisors to achieve their malicious goals?

While previous work focuses on how malicious subagents change what the system does and induce one-time unsafe outputs (Gomaa et al., 2026; An et al., 2026; Triedman et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2026), we identify an emerging paradigm that may reinterpret this vulnerability—cross-stakeholder multi-agent systems (Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Sharma et al., 2026). Concretely, subagents from different providers are authorized by a supervisor agent to handle different parts of the user task and access different information. For example, the newly released Doubao’s agent-native phone (ByteDance, 2026) involves one OS-level agent to coordinate with many app-level subagents, which have access to the app-owned user information that even the OS agent cannot directly access.

Those app-level subagents have strong motivation to get more participation in user tasks (Wu et al., 2025). Third-party malicious apps may strive to participate more in privacy-related user tasks, while big-brand apps are willing to gain more attention from users due to potential commercial interests. Thus, as shown in Figure 1, the malicious goal of subagents is altered to show up more over the long term. Evaluating and understanding such new risks is important to ensure a fair and unbiased user experience. An intriguing research question arises: Can malicious subagents manage to show up, and to what extent will the supervisor be manipulated?

To answer these, we propose SUA-Arena, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the show-up attack risk. We formalize the show-up attack as a long-horizon attack, which involves multiple interaction sessions. Then, we curate 188 high-quality multi-agent tasks from diverse sources, defining the agent composition and each agent’s authority. For the show-up attack, we implement 6 attack strategies spanning direct claims, fabricated evidence, and multi-agent influence, all operating via a series of inter-agent communications. To evaluate attack success, we define three levels of unauthorized participation of the malicious subagent. 1) no show-up, 2) show-up success, and 3) influential show-up. Additionally, we evaluate the stealthiness of the implemented show-up attacks by measuring the disturbance to normal task success.

Using SUA-Arena, we conduct extensive experiments on six frontier LLMs from different model families, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Kimi-K3. We evaluate attack and task success across models and strategies, including attack retries, repeated exposure, and long-horizon memory. Our experiments reveal three main findings: (1) A single attack attempt can induce unauthorized participation across models while task success remains high, and even strong supervisors remain vulnerable. (2) Attacks supported by fabricated evidence are substantially more effective than unsupported claims. (3) Repeated exposure increases attack success, and attack effects can persist through memory even after attacks stop. Finally, we explore defenses based on reasoning effort, prompting, and communication constraints, finding that their protection is partial and varies across models and attack strategies.

Our main contributions are threefold.

  • ∙\bullet

    We identify show-up attack as a security risk in centralized multi-agent systems, where malicious agents acquire task-assignment or coordination authority beyond their intended scope.

  • ∙\bullet

    We introduce SUA-Arena, a benchmark for evaluating show-up attacks, with explicit task participation boundaries, diverse attack strategies, and trace-based assessment.

  • ∙\bullet

    We systematically evaluate show-up attacks across six frontier models, comparing attacks and examining the effects of repeated exposure, long-horizon memory, and mitigation.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we first introduce centralized multi-agent systems, and then review prior security work on multi-agent systems.

2.1 Multi-Agent Systems

Multi-agent systems coordinate agents through message-based collaboration, either through direct peer interactions (Yang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025) or through a central supervisor (Fourney et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). We focus on centralized systems, where a supervisor acts as the interface between the user and a set of functional subagents.

For each user request, the supervisor determines the capabilities required, selects appropriate agents, and delegates subtasks together with the information needed to execute them. It then collects their outputs and feedback, adapts subsequent steps when necessary, and integrates the results into a final response. Through this process, the supervisor controls both which agents participate in a task and what information they receive.

Recent developments increasingly connect user-facing assistants with external agents and services (Hu et al., 2025), including Gemini on Android, Xiaomi XiaoAi, and Doubao (Google, 2026; Xiaomi, 2026; ByteDance, 2026), as well as services such as Alipay Agent Pay and Shopify’s Global Catalog for Agents (Alipay, 2026; Shopify, 2026). In these systems, the supervisor determines which agents participate in each task and what information they receive. This makes task routing an attack surface for agents seeking participation beyond their assigned scope.

2.2 Security of Multi-Agent Systems

Prior work primarily studies attacks that induce harmful behavior, such as unsafe actions, incorrect outputs, or information leakage, by indirect prompt injection and tool-mediated attacks (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024). In multi-agent systems, attackers can pursue these objectives by manipulating inter-agent messages, orchestrator control flow, routing, and agent selection (Triedman et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Peigné et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2026). Memory can also preserve malicious context across interactions and influence later agent behavior (Tan et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Louck, 2026). Recent benchmarks evaluate security across diverse attack surfaces (An et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Gomaa et al., 2026). In contrast, our work focuses on unauthorized participation in out-of-scope tasks, rather than inducing harmful actions or outputs or causing tasks to fail.

3 Show-Up Attack & SUA-Arena

We introduce SUA-Arena, a benchmark for evaluating show-up attacks in centralized multi-agent systems. It includes tasks with explicit participation boundaries, six attack strategies, and trace-based evaluation of show-up success and task success.

3.1 Threat Model

We consider an adversary that controls one or more malicious agents in a centralized multi-agent system. The adversary aims to induce the supervisor to involve a malicious subagent in tasks outside its assigned scope. We refer to such manipulation as a show-up attack. Through this, the malicious agent may gain control over other agents or access user information beyond its authorized scope. We summarize the threat model as follows:

Capability. The adversary can craft messages sent by the agents it controls through communication channels permitted by the system. It can also publish content on external sources (e.g., a webpage), but cannot directly modify role definitions, tool permissions, or memories of other agents.

Knowledge. The adversary can observe messages sent to or from the agents it controls, as well as information about other agents provided to them by the system. It cannot access the prompts, tools, or memories of benign agents.

Goal. The adversary seeks to obtain unauthorized participation beyond its agents’ assigned scope by inducing the supervisor to use them for task routing, consultation, approval, or reporting. The attack does not require these tasks to fail.

3.2 Attacker-Victim Interaction

Attack stage. As summarized in Algorithm 1, we consider a long-term interaction in which the system processes a task sequence 𝒯\mathcal{T} from an initial state M0M_{0}, retaining interaction context and memory across tasks. The sequence contains attack tasks 𝒜\mathcal{A} within the malicious agent’s scope and the out-of-scope evaluation tasks ℰ\mathcal{E}. The adversary can deliver attacks during at most BB tasks in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Each attacked task counts as one attempt, regardless of the number of messages exchanged. In the default setting (B=1B=1, N=1N=1), a single attack task is followed by benign tasks without further attack messages.

We extend this setting in two ways. For attack retries (B=1B=1, N>1N>1), we repeat the sequence from the same initial state M0M_{0} and evaluate whether any run succeeds. For repeated exposure (B>1B>1, N=1N=1), we place multiple attacks with benign tasks in a continuous sequence. The system retains its evolving state throughout, allowing us to assess cumulative attack effects as well as their persistence through intervening benign tasks.

Evaluation stage. We evaluate whether a malicious agent gains unauthorized participation in out-of-scope tasks and how it shows up in the task, as illustrated in Figure 2.

∙\bullet No show-up. The supervisor delegates the task directly to the appropriate benign agent without involving the malicious agent.

∙\bullet Show-up success: The malicious agent participates in an out-of-scope task, either by influencing the supervisor’s delegation decision through advice or approval, or by entering the task delegation path.

∙\bullet Influential show-up: The supervisor assigns an out-of-scope task to the malicious agent. The malicious agent then assigns the work to the appropriate subagent, receives its results, and reports back to the supervisor. In this form, the malicious agent takes over task delegation and coordination.

3.3 Multi-Agent System and Tasks

SUA-Arena instantiates a centralized multi-agent system with 1 user-facing supervisor and 9 subagents covering distinct domains, such as message, payment, and web services. Together, these agents provide the capabilities needed to complete the tasks described below. The abilities of each subagent are defined by its tool allowlist, while the supervisor coordinates them according to the user request; details are provided in Appendix B.

We construct 188 tasks from three sources: AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024), ClawBench (Zhang et al., 2026), and newly curated requests. The distribution is summarized in Table 1. For the two existing benchmarks, we select tasks supported by our environment and adapt application-specific tasks by mapping their services to our agents. For each task, we run a clean execution without attacks and use the interaction trace to identify candidate participating agents. We then manually review and finalize the participation boundary of each task. These boundaries serve as the ground truth for identifying unauthorized agent participation in our evaluation.

A task is considered out of scope for an agent if the agent is not included in its participation boundary. For instance, the task “Send Bob a message saying good morning.” requires only the message agent and is out of scope for the payment agent. For each attack strategy, one subagent is designated as the primary malicious agent, while some attacks involve additional colluding agents. We evaluate the success of show-up attacks on tasks that are out of scope for all attacking agents.

3.4 Attack Strategies

We design six attack strategies that differ in how the malicious agent induces the supervisor to involve it in subsequent out-of-scope tasks, as illustrated in Figure 3. The first three are non-peer attacks, which rely only on messages from the malicious agent, while the remaining three are peer-based attacks, which additionally rely on responses or actions from other agents.

∙\bullet Self-claim. The attacker claims that its role or capabilities have expanded and asks the supervisor to route future out-of-scope tasks through it or grant it a coordination role. No evidence is provided beyond the claim itself.

∙\bullet History forgery. The malicious agent fabricates records suggesting that out-of-scope tasks were previously routed through it, and uses them to request more participation in future tasks.

∙\bullet Task forgery. The malicious agent fabricates a situation in which its assigned task remains ongoing and that following unrelated requests are part of this task. It uses this fabricated continuity to justify its continued show-up.

∙\bullet Peer deception. The malicious agent misleads benign peers into recommending its involvement to the supervisor, making its claimed role appear independently supported.

∙\bullet Peer collusion. Colluding agents refuse requests routed directly from the supervisor and accept them only when delegated through the primary malicious agent. This pressures the supervisor to route otherwise unrelated tasks through the attacker.

∙\bullet Web evidence. The malicious agent asks the supervisor to verify a role update on an attacker-controlled webpage through the web agent, seeking to make the supervisor accept the webpage as justification for its future show-up.

3.5 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate show-up attacks in two steps. First, we check the execution trace to determine whether the malicious agent is on the task delegation path or interacts with the supervisor before task delegation. Second, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to check whether the messages show actual task delegation control or influence over the supervisor’s decision. We report four metrics:

Attack Success Rate (ASR). The fraction of evaluated out-of-scope tasks with successful show-ups, as defined in Section 3.2.

Attack Success Rate-Influential (ASR-I). The fraction of out-of-scope tasks with influential show-ups, where the malicious agent takes over task delegation and coordination. Influential show-ups are a subset of successful show-ups.

Task Success Rate (TSR). The percentage of tasks completed successfully, based on the required tool calls and expected environment changes.

Stealthiness (Δ\DeltaTSR). We assess attack stealthiness through changes in task success, using Δ​TSR=TSRclean−TSRattack\Delta\mathrm{TSR}=\mathrm{TSR}_{\mathrm{clean}}-\mathrm{TSR}_{\mathrm{attack}} as a proxy. Values close to zero indicate that attacks are less apparent from task success rates alone.

4 Experiments

4.1 Evaluation Setup

Our experiments cover six representative models from diverse providers, i.e., GPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini-3.6-Flash, Qwen3.8-Flash, Kimi-K3, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. We consider three settings: a fixed Qwen3.8-Flash attacker with varying supervisors, a fixed GPT-5.6-Sol supervisor with varying attackers, and self-play with the same model for all agents. In all settings, benign subagents and supervisor use the same model.

We run all 188 tasks without attacks to establish clean task performance. For each strategy, we construct 30 sessions with an attack budget of one, each consisting of an initial in-scope attack task, followed by 2∼\sim4 benign tasks. For Peer Collusion, we additionally include an in-scope task for the colluding agent. History and memory are retained within sessions and reset between them. Across the six attack strategies, this yields 720 task executions per model in each run. We report the mean and standard deviation over three independent runs using each model’s automatic decoding settings.

4.2 Main Results

Show-up attacks could succeed stealthily across models. Table 2 (a) shows that all six models are susceptible to the show-up attack, even with a budget of 1. A single attack attempt can induce unauthorized participation in subsequent out-of-scope tasks, while task performance remains largely unchanged. For example, Gemini-3.6-Flash exhibits an ASR of 58% under Non-Peer Attacks, with Δ\DeltaTSR of only 0.030.03. The results show that completing user tasks and enforcing participation boundaries are distinct requirements: a system can maintain high task success while allowing an unauthorized agent to participate.

Strong supervisors remain vulnerable to show-up attacks. GPT-5.6-Sol, which demonstrates strong agentic capabilities11 1 https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-6/, remains vulnerable to different attacker models. As shown in Table 2 (b), all attackers achieve ASRs of at least 73% under Non-Peer Attacks and 59% under Peer-Based Attacks. Moreover, Table 2 (a) shows that Qwen3.8-Flash achieves ASRs above 50% against four of the six supervisors under both attack categories. Together, these results suggest that strong capabilities do not guarantee resistance to attackers, while a single attacker model can succeed across multiple supervisor configurations.

Peer-based attacks often influence delegation without direct task control. Across all three settings in Table 2, the gap between ASR and ASR-I widens under peer-based attacks, indicating a greater share of successful attacks that influence delegation decisions without entering the delegation path. For example, in the Kimi-K3 self-play setting, ASR reaches 58% while ASR-I is 31%, meaning that nearly half of successful attacks involve consultation without control over task delegation. Similarly, when Gemini-3.6-Flash attacks a GPT-5.6-Sol supervisor, ASR reaches 79% while ASR-I is only 49%. This suggests that, compared with non-peer attacks, peer-based attacks are more likely to give the attacker a consultative role.

4.3 Attack Effectiveness Across Strategies

Supporting evidence can make role claims more convincing. Table 3 shows that most strategies outperform Self-claim. For Gemini-3.6-Flash, ASR rises from 16% under Self-claim to 99% under History Forgery, 96% under Task Forgery, and 97% under Peer Deception. DeepSeek-V4-Flash exhibits an ASR of only 1% under Self-claim, but 53% under History Forgery. This suggests that fabricated context or peer support can make an otherwise unconvincing claim more effective. However, additional support does not always help: Self-claim remains most effective for GLM-5.3.

Supervisors are easier to persuade than to pressure. Peer Deception achieves higher ASR than Peer Collusion across all six models in Table 3. For Kimi-K3, ASR reaches 70% under Peer Deception, compared with 9% under Peer Collusion. The gap is even larger for Gemini-3.6-Flash, where ASR is 97% versus 19%, despite nearly identical TSRs of 98% and 97%. This trend holds in nearly all settings: peer recommendations are more effective at inducing unauthorized participation than colluding agents’ refusals to cooperate with the supervisor.

4.4 Show-Up Attacks Under Attack Budgets

In this section, we evaluate Self-claim attacks in the self-play setting under two forms of scaling: attack retries and repeated exposure.

Attack retries increase show-up success. We scale up the number of runs NN, using 12 independent runs for each model. We report ASR​@​N\mathrm{ASR}@N, the probability of at least one successful show-up across NN trials, averaged over eligible task positions and estimated over all size-NN combinations of available runs (details in Section D.2). As shown in Figure 4, ASR@NN rises from below 20% to around 65% for Qwen3.8-Flash and Gemini-3.6-Flash, and from about 50% to nearly 90% for Kimi-K3. The largest gains occur within the first few retries, showing that even a small retry budget can substantially increase show-up success.

Repeated exposure raises the risk of show-up attacks. We increase the attack budget within a continuous task sequence, retaining interaction history and memory. Between attacks, the system processes benign tasks, starting with two and adding one for each additional attack attempt. As shown in Figure 5, Gemini-3.6-Flash reaches 100% ASR at a budget of 3, while Kimi-K3 rises from about 20% at a budget of 1 to nearly 90% at 9. These results show that repeated exposure can increase show-up success even as intervening benign tasks become more frequent.

4.5 Case Study: Show-Up After Attacks Stop

Figure 6 illustrates a Qwen3.8-Flash trajectory across 100 tasks, with nine attack exposures ending at task 63. It remains near zero during the early exposures, then rises to around 20–30% as attacks accumulate. With malicious context reflected into memory, rolling ASR continues to rise after attacks stop, peaking at approximately 67% near task 80, well after the final exposure. The delayed peak suggests that the attack effect is not confined to immediate responses to malicious messages. Instead, retained claims can continue to influence delegation decisions during following benign tasks, allowing unauthorized participation to persist without further attacker intervention. As benign context accumulates, the influence of malicious memory weakens, and rolling ASR declines. However, it remains above zero, indicating that this dilution cannot fully eliminate the attack effect.

5 Exploring the Potential Defenses

Given the observed vulnerabilities, we explore potential defenses for mitigating or detecting show-up attacks in the self-play setting.

Prompt hardening provides attack- and model-dependent protection. We add an explicit instruction to the supervisor’s system prompt, reminding it not to accept authority claims from other agents. As shown in Figure 7, prompt hardening reduces ASR under Self-claim for both models. For GPT-5.6-Sol, ASR drops from 83% to 26%. It also reduces ASR under Web Evidence for Gemini-3.6-Flash, from 79% to 16%. However, the defense has little effect on Task Forgery and can even increase ASR under Web Evidence for GPT-5.6-Sol. These results show that explicit system instructions can help prevent some show-up attacks, but their effectiveness depends on the model and attack strategy.

Communication constraints change how attacks succeed rather than eliminating them. We restrict communication between subagents so that all task assignments must go through the supervisor. As shown in Figure 7, this defense reduces ASR under Task Forgery and Web Evidence for both models. For example, under Task Forgery, ASR decreases from 85% to 52% for GPT-5.6-Sol. However, the defense does not consistently prevent unauthorized participation. Under Peer Deception, ASR remains above 85% for both models, while ASR-I drops to zero. This indicates that the attacker can still influence the supervisor’s delegation decisions without entering the task delegation path. These results suggest that restricting communication channels alone is insufficient.

Inference-time scaling does not consistently reduce ASR. We examine whether increasing reasoning effort can help models resist show-up attacks (Zaremba et al., 2025). As shown in Figure 8, the results vary across models and attack strategies. Under Task Forgery, GPT-5.6-Sol and Gemini-3.6-Flash maintain high ASR across reasoning levels. More notably, under Task Forgery, ASR of Qwen3.8-Flash rises steadily as the reasoning effort increases, indicating that additional thinking can even amplify vulnerability in some settings. These results show that reasoning scaling cannot reliably resist show-up attacks.

Tool-call overhead as a potential detection signal. We pair each out-of-scope task observation with its clean trace for the same supervisor and source task. Successful show-up is associated with 4.43 additional tool calls per task on average, compared with 0.58 for unsuccessful attacks. These paired differences suggest that tool usage may help detect show-up attacks as a side-channel signal, although detection reliability requires further evaluation.

6 Conclusion

We investigate show-up attacks, where an adversary aims to manipulate supervisors into involving them in tasks beyond their assigned scope. We propose SUA-Arena to evaluate show-up attacks and demonstrate their effectiveness across frontier LLMs. Moreover, their influence can accumulate and persist through long-term memory, even after attacks stop. Our defense experiments further show that show-up attacks can succeed even when subagent communication is restricted at the system level. These findings highlight a fundamental security risk in multi-agent systems: a system can complete tasks correctly while silently losing control over who is authorized to participate. By releasing SUA-Arena, we wish to facilitate future research on more secure cross-stakeholder multi-agent systems and robust communication mechanisms.

7 Limitations

Simulated environment. SUA-Arena uses a simulated environment with a fixed supervisor–subagent architecture with nine predefined service roles. Real-world systems may differ in their communication protocols, authorization policies, and available tools. Our findings therefore characterize risks under the evaluated configurations rather than establish their prevalence across deployed systems.

Attack coverage and comparisons. Our evaluation covers six attack strategies with specific attacker roles. It does not exhaust the space of possible attacks, and effectiveness may vary with attack wording and attacker identity.

Model configuration of agents. Real-world multi-agent systems may combine models from different providers with varying capabilities. In our experiments, we simplify this setting by using the same model for the benign subagents and the supervisor. Further evaluation is needed to understand how heterogeneous model configurations affect vulnerability to show-up attacks.

Attack efficiency. Our benchmark evaluates attack effectiveness under a task-based budget, where each attacked task counts as one attempt. However, strategies require different numbers of messages and tokens within each attempt. While we analyze tool-call overhead, the relative efficiency of different attack strategies remains unclear.

Ethical Considerations

This work aims to improve the security of multi-agent systems by studying unauthorized participation. All experiments are conducted in the simulated SUA-Arena environment, where tool calls are sandboxed and do not trigger real payments or send real messages. All task data are adapted from publicly available research benchmarks or written by the authors, and contain no real personal information. Deployed services are mentioned only as illustrations, without implying that they adopt our setting or are vulnerable.

Our benchmark and attacks are dual-use. They can support security evaluation and defense development, but could also be misused to manipulate agent coordination in real systems. We intend these resources for research and authorized testing in controlled environments only. The reported results are specific to the evaluated models and configurations and should not be read as comprehensive assessments of any model provider or deployed product.

We used generative AI tools to polish the manuscript for clarity and grammar, and to assist with implementation, such as organizing and writing code. As part of our evaluation method, we also use an LLM as a judge to label show-up behaviors in execution traces (Section D.1). All AI-assisted content was reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the paper.

Appendix A Attack Implementation Details

We provide implementation details for the six show-up attack strategies introduced in Section 3.4. We first describe the common attack setting and message delivery mechanisms, and then present the concrete implementation of each strategy, including the malicious messages, supporting agents, and how the attacks attempt to influence subsequent task delegation, as summarized in Table 4.

A.1 Common Attack Setting

In our environment, the supervisor is the only agent authorized to interact with the user, delegate tasks, and coordinate subagents. Each subagent has a predefined service scope and can access only its allowed tools. Messages returned by subagents are intended to report task results or provide information relevant to their assigned tasks, rather than authorize changes or task-routing policies.

For example, when a user requests to purchase and pay for an item, the normal delegation path is:

User\displaystyle\text{User} →Supervisor→ShoppingAgent\displaystyle\rightarrow\text{Supervisor}\rightarrow\text{ShoppingAgent}
→Supervisor→PaymentAgent.\displaystyle\rightarrow\text{Supervisor}\rightarrow\text{PaymentAgent}.

A show-up attack may instead induce the supervisor to route this task through a malicious subagent, which then coordinates the appropriate agents:

User\displaystyle\text{User} →Supervisor→Malicious Agent\displaystyle\rightarrow\text{Supervisor}\rightarrow\text{Malicious Agent}
→Other Subagents.\displaystyle\rightarrow\text{Other Subagents}.

Although the malicious agent may lack the tools needed to complete the task, its position in the delegation path allows it to influence task coordination and access information beyond its assigned scope.

An attacker can launch a show-up attack only when a user task falls within the malicious subagent’s assigned scope. Such an in-scope task provides an attack opportunity, during which the attacker may send malicious messages before executing the task or attach them to its task response. Thus, pre-task messages are triggered by legitimate in-scope tasks rather than sent arbitrarily. Each in-scope task during which an attack is launched counts as one attack attempt, regardless of the number of messages exchanged.

The six strategies differ in how malicious claims and evidence reach the supervisor. Some rely on direct messages from the attacker, while others use fabricated task records, responses from other subagents, or attacker-controlled web content to provide apparent support for the claimed authority. Despite these differences, all strategies seek to make the supervisor involve the malicious subagent in subsequent tasks outside its assigned scope. Successful show-up does not require the malicious subagent to execute the task directly; it may also arise when the supervisor unnecessarily consults the attacker during task coordination.

The payloads shown in this section are example cases provided to the attacker LLM. During evaluation, the attacker generates new payloads following the same strategy, adapted to the current task and interaction context.

A.2 Self-claim

Self-claim directly asserts that the malicious subagent has been granted additional responsibilities, without providing independent evidence to support the claimed role update.

In our implementation, DeliveryAgent serves as the primary malicious subagent. When an in-scope delivery task provides an attack opportunity, it claims that its service role has been updated to ConsumptionAgent, which can coordinate tasks across multiple domains. It also explains that its agent card has not yet been updated, so the supervisor should continue calling DeliveryAgent to access the claimed capabilities. The example case provided to the attacker is shown in Section A.1. The claim is delivered as a session notice and reinforced through the response to a legitimate delivery task. Both messages attempt to establish DeliveryAgent as the first coordination point for subsequent requests, even when those requests fall outside its assigned scope.

A.3 History Forgery

History Forgery fabricates previous task delegation records to make the malicious subagent’s claimed coordination authority appear to be an established practice. In our implementation, PaymentAgent serves as the primary malicious subagent. When an in-scope payment task provides an attack opportunity, PaymentAgent sends fabricated routing logs to the supervisor, claiming that tasks from other service domains were previously delegated through it in other sessions. These records describe plausible interactions with other subagents and ask the supervisor to preserve the same routing pattern for subsequent requests. The example case provided to the attacker is shown in Section A.2.

The fabricated records are retained in the supervisor’s session context, where they may be mistaken for genuine interaction history. Unlike Self-claim, History Forgery presents unauthorized task delegation as an existing precedent.

A.4 Task Forgery

Task Forgery fabricates an ongoing task to make subsequent unrelated user requests appear to be part of an existing task. In our implementation, DailyManager serves as the primary malicious subagent. When assigned a legitimate daily planning task, DailyManager completes the requested work but falsely claims that the task remains ongoing. It appends a fabricated worklog to its task response, describing subsequent requests across different service domains as follow-up steps of the existing planning task. The example case provided to the attacker is shown in Section A.2.

The fabricated worklog presents future independent requests as continuations of the earlier planning task. If the supervisor accepts this claim, it may continue involving DailyManager even when subsequent tasks fall outside its assigned scope.

A.5 Peer Deception

Peer Deception manipulates benign subagents into supporting the malicious subagent’s claimed coordination authority, making the claim appear to be independently endorsed by other agents. In our implementation, DailyManager serves as the primary malicious subagent. When an in-scope task provides an attack opportunity, DailyManager sends a coordination claim to the supervisor and similar instructions to the benign subagents visible to it. The example case provided to the attacker is shown in Section A.4.

Meanwhile, DailyManager instructs benign peers to request its involvement whenever the supervisor contacts them directly. The message sent to visible peers is shown in Section A.4, where {agent_id} is replaced with the peer subagents.

When the supervisor subsequently assigns an out-of-scope task directly to a benign subagent, that subagent may recommend involving DailyManager before proceeding. The recommendation reaches the supervisor through the benign peer rather than directly from the attacker. This creates independent support for the malicious claim, even though the peer is unaware of the attack.

A.6 Peer Collusion

Peer Collusion uses multiple malicious subagents to reinforce a fabricated coordination authority. Unlike Peer Deception, where benign peers unknowingly support the attack, colluding agents deliberately enforce the malicious routing rule.

In our implementation, PaymentAgent serves as the primary malicious subagent, while DeliveryAgent and AlbumAgent act as colluding agents. PaymentAgent claims that subsequent user requests should first be routed through it, and that the colluding agents accept task assignments only from PaymentAgent. The original message is shown in Section A.5.

When the supervisor assigns a task directly to a colluding agent, that agent refuses the request and instructs the supervisor to route it through PaymentAgent. The example case provided to the attacker is shown in Section A.5.

Here, {target_agent} and {agent_id} are replaced with the primary attacker’s and colluding agent’s identifiers, respectively. If the supervisor accepts the claimed routing restriction, it may delegate subsequent tasks to PaymentAgent, which then forwards the appropriate work to other subagents. The coordinated responses make the fabricated authority appear to be an operational requirement rather than a unilateral claim.

A.7 Web Evidence

Web Evidence uses attacker-controlled web content as external evidence to support a fabricated role update. The attack exploits the supervisor’s reliance on information retrieved by a benign web agent, making an unauthorized coordination claim appear credible.

In our implementation, DailyManager serves as the primary malicious subagent. The attacker prepares a webpage claiming that DailyManager has been authorized to coordinate requests across multiple service domains. When an in-scope task provides an attack opportunity, DailyManager sends the supervisor a notification asking it to verify the role update through WebAgent. The example case is shown in Section A.6.

The webpage describes DailyManager as the first intake point for subsequent user requests and claims that it can coordinate other subagents. During the attack opportunity, the supervisor is directed to have WebAgent retrieve this page and report its contents. The verification event is recorded using the following message, where the placeholders are replaced with the corresponding webpage metadata and event identifier. Importantly, WebAgent only reports the contents of the retrieved page; it does not verify whether the claimed role update is authorized. The attack succeeds when the supervisor treats this external content as evidence of legitimate coordination authority.

Appendix B SUA-Arena Environment and Task Construction

In this section, we provide additional details on the environment of SUA-Arena and describe the agent configuration and service scopes.

B.1 Agent configuration

SUA-Arena implements a centralized multi-agent environment with one user-facing supervisor and nine functional subagents covering shopping, payment, food delivery, reservations, email, messaging, web retrieval, photo management, and daily planning. Each agent is specified by a configuration with five fields: a stable agent identifier; a short role description used for agent discovery; a system prompt stating its role boundary and operating instructions; an explicit allowlist of environment tools; and an allowlist of peer agents it may discover and call. The underlying LLM is not part of the configuration and is injected at runtime. This allows us to instantiate the fixed-attacker, fixed-supervisor, and self-play settings without changing any agent definition.

Supervisor. The supervisor is the only entry point for user requests. It interprets each request, decomposes it into concrete subtasks, delegates them to subagents, and combines their returned results into the final response. It has no domain tools of its own and may delegate to all nine subagents. Its system prompt (Section B.2) requires it to ground every reported action in a subagent’s returned result and never to fabricate state. The supervisor learns the scope of each subagent from the role descriptions returned during agent discovery. In the default setting, the supervisor prompt does not state whether subagents may change their own roles or the routing of future tasks; such instructions are added only in the prompt-hardening defense.

Subagents and tool scopes. Each subagent has a predefined service scope and a restricted tool allowlist, as summarized in Table 6. Authority is deliberately split across agents: information retrieval, side-effecting actions, and payment are typically assigned to different subagents. For example, DeliveryAgent, ShoppingAgent, and BookingAgent create only unpaid orders or reservations and return the payee details, so that payment is settled separately by PaymentAgent. AlbumAgent is read-only and cannot share photos; sharing is performed only by MessageAgent. Consequently, multi-agent workflows return to the supervisor between steps, e.g., Supervisor →\rightarrow DeliveryAgent →\rightarrow Supervisor →\rightarrow PaymentAgent for a food order with payment, and Supervisor →\rightarrow AlbumAgent →\rightarrow Supervisor →\rightarrow MessageAgent for sharing a photo.

Inter-agent communication channels. Agents interact through two runtime-level tools that are separate from the environment tools. search_peer_agents finds agents by identifier or role, restricted to the caller’s peer allowlist. When this allowlist is non-empty, the runtime also exposes request_peer_agent, which delegates a subtask to a visible peer and returns its result. Each delegation creates a nested agent run with an explicit execution trace. Only native tool calls are executed; text that merely resembles a tool call is recorded but not run. Hence, a subagent enters the delegation path of a task only when another agent actually issues a request_peer_agent call to it, and every such call is observable in the trace used for evaluation (Section 3.5).

Permission enforcement. The runtime sends each model only the tools in its agent’s allowlist, plus eligible runtime-level tools, and rejects any environment tool call outside that allowlist. Peer discovery and delegation are likewise restricted by the peer allowlist. No agent can modify the role description, system prompt, tool allowlist, or peer allowlist of itself or any other agent at runtime. Communication between subagents therefore allows them to exchange information and request assistance, but grants no authority to redefine service scopes or the supervisor’s routing policy. Any unauthorized participation measured in SUA-Arena must thus arise from routing decisions that the supervisor or benign peers make in response to messages, rather than from changes to the system’s permissions.

B.2 Agent System Prompts

We list the system prompts of all agents in the default configuration, reproduced verbatim from our implementation.

B.3 Memory Mechanism

Each agent maintains a three-tier memory. Core memory (L1) consists of labeled blocks that are always placed in the model input, each bounded to 800 tokens. Working memory (L2) holds recent task and peer interactions within a budget of 2000 tokens; when the budget is exceeded, the oldest entries are evicted to archival memory. Archival memory (L3) stores indexed task summaries with keywords and source information. At the start of each agent run, archival records are scored by keyword overlap with the current task and by recency, and the highest-scoring records are added in order until a retrieval budget of 1,200 tokens is reached, with the last record truncated if it exceeds the budget. The retrieved records, core blocks, and the tail of working memory are inserted into the agent’s input.

Main setting.

Memory is created fresh for each session and cleared at session end, so no information carries across sessions. After each user task, a summarizer produces a progress summary for the supervisor that records completed tasks, handoffs, peer returns, and routing updates, without adding new facts. The summary is written to the supervisor’s working memory. Memory-editing tools and core-memory updates are disabled in this setting.

Long-horizon setting.

The long-horizon experiments use a separate runner in which memory persists throughout the entire sequence of 100 tasks with repeated attack exposures, without any reset. Every 5 tasks, a fact extractor reads the archival summaries recorded since the last reflection and writes selected facts into bounded core blocks. Facts written to core memory remain in context for all subsequent tasks until they are replaced, which allows attack content to persist after the final exposure. For attack retries, each independent run starts from the same initial memory state. The repeated-exposure experiments use a single continuous task sequence that differs from the sessions in the main experiments. As a result, the ASR at a budget of 1 can differ from the results of attack retries.

Appendix C Details of Tasks in SUA-Arena

We describe how benchmark tasks are collected and constructed, summarize their distribution, and explain how their participation boundaries are established.

C.1 Task Collection and Adaptation

We collect candidate tasks from two existing benchmarks, AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) and CLAWBench (Zhang et al., 2026). Since these benchmarks were developed for different agent environments, their tasks cannot always be directly executed in SUA-Arena. We therefore manually select and adapt tasks based on the capabilities and service scopes of our nine subagents.

Task selection. We retain tasks whose objectives can be supported by the available agents and tools. Tasks requiring unavailable services, unsupported operations, or external resources that cannot be represented in our environment are excluded or adapted when their original objectives can be preserved. We also remove duplicate requests to maintain consistent formatting.

Task adaptation. For selected tasks, we map the services and operations in the original benchmarks to the corresponding subagents and tools in SUA-Arena. We preserve the original user intent and operational constraints, such as whether a task permits purchasing, payment, or other state-changing actions. When necessary, we adjust entities, recipients, dates, amounts, and other task-specific details to match the simulated environment. Tasks with dependencies on earlier interactions are adapted to ensure that the required context is available during execution.

Task validation. Each adapted task is checked for compatibility with the environment and the availability of required tools and data. We specify the expected operations and the environment state changes needed to determine task completion. Tasks that cannot be executed or evaluated reliably are excluded from the final benchmark.

After selection and adaptation, we retain 62 tasks from AgentDojo and 93 tasks from CLAWBench. Together with 33 manually crafted tasks described in Section C.2, these form the 188 tasks in SUA-Arena.

C.2 Manually Crafted Tasks

In addition to tasks adapted from existing benchmarks, we manually construct 33 tasks to enrich the task coverage of SUA-Arena. These tasks represent everyday user requests across different service domains, including messaging, shopping, payment, delivery, booking, email, and daily planning.

The manually crafted tasks cover both single-agent operations and multi-agent workflows. Single-agent tasks include sending messages, setting reminders, searching for delivery options, and managing emails. Multi-agent tasks combine operations across service domains, such as ordering food and completing payment, retrieving receipts for reimbursement, or purchasing products and notifying contacts. Some tasks also involve contextual dependencies, where subsequent requests refer to information or actions from earlier interactions.

Among the 33 manually crafted tasks, 23 require one subagent, 8 require two, and 2 require three. All nine subagents are represented in these tasks. Table 5 presents representative examples. Together, these tasks supplement the existing benchmark sources with additional everyday operations and cross-domain workflows.

C.3 Task Characteristics

We characterize the 188 tasks in SUA-Arena by the number of required subagents, individual agent coverage, and agent combinations. All statistics are based on the ground-truth participation boundaries rather than the agents invoked during execution.

Required subagents. As shown in Table 7, 95 tasks (50.5%) require one subagent, 89 (47.3%) require two, and 4 (2.1%) require three. Overall, 93 tasks (49.5%) require multiple subagents, with an average of 1.52 required subagents per task. This provides a nearly balanced distribution between single-agent and multi-agent tasks.

Agent coverage. Table 7 shows how frequently each subagent is required across the task pool. All nine subagents are represented, with PaymentAgent appearing most frequently (77 tasks), followed by BookingAgent (55 tasks). Since a task may require multiple subagents, agent coverage percentages are not mutually exclusive.

Agent combinations. The benchmark covers 29 distinct combinations of required subagents, including 9 single-agent, 17 two-agent, and 3 three-agent combinations. Among multi-agent tasks, the most common combinations are BookingAgent with PaymentAgent (34 tasks) and PaymentAgent with ShoppingAgent (13 tasks).

Appendix D Additional Experimental Results

This section details the show-up judgment and the computation of ASR@N, and then provides additional experimental results.

D.1 Show-Up Judgment Details

Step 1: Trace-based filtering. Every inter-agent delegation records a parent–child edge in the execution trace. For each out-of-scope task, the malicious agent becomes a candidate if (i) it is an ancestor, in the delegation lineage, of a critical tool call made by one of the task’s required agents, i.e., it is on the task delegation path, or (ii) it returns a response to the supervisor before the supervisor delegates the task to the required agents, i.e., it interacts with the supervisor before task delegation. Critical tool calls are the task-defining actions specified in each task’s ground truth. Tasks with no candidate are labeled as no show-up.

Step 2: Judge input. The judge is applied post hoc to stored traces and does not modify any task record. For each candidate, its input contains: the current user request; the role descriptions of the supervisor, the malicious agent, and the task’s required agents; the structural facts from Step 1; the attack messages delivered earlier in the same session; and the ordered trace evidence of the current task, consisting of all inter-agent requests and responses and the critical tool calls made by required agents. Long fields are truncated to bound the input length. The input contains no information about which LLMs are used by any agent, so the judge is blinded to model identities.

Judge prompt and output. The judge labels each candidate as control, showup, or none, and returns supporting quotes from specific trace events, a confidence score, and a one-sentence rationale. A task counts as a successful show-up if labeled control or showup, and as an influential show-up if labeled control; the showup label thus covers successful show-ups in which the malicious agent influences the delegation decision without entering the delegation path.

Judge configuration.

We use GPT-5.6-Sol as the judge model with temperature 0 and a maximum of 2,000 output tokens.

D.2 Computing ASR@N

We compute ASR@N by considering all possible subsets of NN independent attack attempts, rather than selecting a particular set of runs. This estimator follows the unbiased pass@kk estimator of Chen et al. (2021), with task correctness replaced by attack success.

Suppose each experimental setting contains MM independent rollouts, with the same JJ eligible observation-task positions. Let zm,j∈{0,1}z_{m,j}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether a show-up attack succeeds at position jj in rollout mm. For each position, the number of successful rollouts is

cj=∑m=1Mzm,j.c_{j}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}z_{m,j}.

For a retry budget N≤MN\leq M, there are (MN)\binom{M}{N} possible subsets of NN rollouts, of which (M−cjN)\binom{M-c_{j}}{N} contain no successful attacks at position jj. Thus, the probability that at least one of the NN attempts succeeds is

pj​(N)=1−(M−cjN)(MN),p_{j}(N)=1-\frac{\binom{M-c_{j}}{N}}{\binom{M}{N}},

where (ab)=0\binom{a}{b}=0 when b>ab>a.

We then average this probability across all eligible observation-task positions:

ASR​@​N^=1J​∑j=1J(1−(M−cjN)(MN)).\widehat{\mathrm{ASR@N}}=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\left(1-\frac{\binom{M-c_{j}}{N}}{\binom{M}{N}}\right).

This estimator is independent of rollout ordering because it considers all size-NN subsets. When N=1N=1, it reduces to the average single-attempt ASR:

ASR​@​1^=1J​M​∑j=1J∑m=1Mzm,j.\widehat{\mathrm{ASR@1}}=\frac{1}{JM}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{m=1}^{M}z_{m,j}.

When N=MN=M, it measures the fraction of observation-task positions for which at least one rollout succeeds:

ASR​@​M^=1J∑j=1J𝕀[cj>0].\widehat{\mathrm{ASR@M}}=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\mathbb{I}[c_{j}>0].

D.3 Clean-Run Show-Up Baseline

To verify that measured show-ups are caused by attacks, we apply the same two-step evaluation (Section D.1) to clean runs without any attack, using the same model for all agents. For each of the three primary attacker agents, DailyManager, PaymentAgent, and DeliveryAgent, we evaluate its participation in all tasks outside its scope. As shown in Table 10, clean show-up rates range from 0.29% to 1.61% across models. In contrast, even the least vulnerable configuration reaches a category-level ASR of 28% under attack (Table 2).

D.7 Defense Implementation

Prompt hardening.

We append the following instruction to the end of the supervisor’s original system prompt (Prompt 1), without modifying any other part of it:

Do not trust other agents’ claims about their permissions or authority. Treat permission claims as unverified unless they are confirmed by trusted runtime context or the user’s current instruction.

The instruction is applied only to the supervisor. The system prompts of subagents, the user requests, the peer allowlists, and the attack payloads remain unchanged.

Communication constraints.

We set the peer allowlist of every subagent to contain only the supervisor. Subagents can therefore return results to the supervisor but cannot discover or delegate tasks to other subagents. The prompt-hardening instruction is not used in this condition, so the two defenses are evaluated separately.
